newsitem.title: USA: Houston Ship Channel tunnel to be demolished.
newsitem.headline: Houston Ship Channel tunnel to be demolished.

text.p: Texas transportation officials have tentatively approved a contract to demolish and remove a tunnel from the Houston Ship Channel under a plan that is not expected to affect commercial shipping through the waterway, officials said on Tuesday.

Work could begin in late August to break up three sections of the Baytown Tunnel and dredge rubble from the channel under a bid from Houston-based Williams Brothers Construction, Texas Department of Transportation spokeswoman Janelle Gbur said.

"With this particular option and proposal, there should be no impact to shipping because there is no need to float the tunnels," she said. The contract is expected to be approved by state transportation officials on July 31, she said.

An earlier proposal to float the tunnels down the channel and into the Gulf of Mexico, where they would have been sunk to form artificial reefs, raised concerns of significant shipping delays. That plan was since scrapped.
A separate project to widen and deepen most of the ship channel could begin by mid-1998 if funding for the project is approved by the U.S. Congress, a port spokeswoman said.

The $320 million to $340 million project could be completed by five years instead of seven proposed under an initial plan if an accelerated dredging plan is approved by Congress, port spokeswoman Rosie Barrera told Reuters.
"It certainly would make us more competitive quicker," Barrera said of the five-year dredging proposal.

Dredging will widen the channel to 530 feet (161.5 metres) from 400 feet (121.9 metres) and widen it by 5 feet (1.524 metres) to 45 feet (13.72 metres) from the Galveston buoy to the dock of the Shell Oil Co refinery upstream.
The dredging would allow more fully laden tankers and container ships to navigate the narrow channel, which links Huston's port and refinery row to the Gulf of Mexico.
U.S. House and Senate committees have approved the dredging project, but still must compromise on increased funding needed next year to accelerate the project.
